stories.author: cmrdporcupine
stories.title: Mercury 3: Diffusion at scale
stories.groq_label: Mercury 3 uses a diffusion architecture to deliver over 1,000 tokens per second and a 1 million‑token context while claiming benchmark superiority over leading models.
stories.groq_discussion: This diffusion‑based language model aims to solve the problem of generating text quickly and at large context lengths by using a diffusion architecture instead of a traditional transformer. The Hacker News discussion was generally mixed, with many commenters appreciating the model’s impressive speed (over 1,000 tokens per second), low cost, and large 1 M‑token context, and noting that it appears to match or surpass frontier models such as GPT‑6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on benchmark quality. At the same time, several commenters raised concerns about practical limitations: latency is still slower than some existing services (e.g., DeepSeek v4.1 on OpenRouter), the lack of open‑weight releases makes experimentation difficult, and the non‑linear token generation raises questions about interpretability and reasoning. Overall, the community sees promise in Mercury 3 as a fast, high‑throughput LLM, but believes its impact will depend on addressing openness, performance consistency, and usability challenges.

stories.author: groar
stories.title: Timestral: Mistral's time-series foundation models
stories.groq_label: Timestral positions itself as a universal foundation model that can ingest known‑future covariates and scale to forecast thousands of heterogeneous time‑series with a single architecture.
stories.groq_discussion:
Discussion type: – Balanced:

This foundation‑model‑based product, Timestral, aims to solve the problem of building accurate, scalable forecasts for large collections of time‑series data. The Hacker News discussion was generally mixed, with many commenters appreciating its strengths—particularly the ability to train a single model that can handle thousands of series, the impressive speed and ease of use (e.g., “minutes instead of months” to get good results), and performance that approaches state‑of‑the‑art benchmarks. At the same time, several commenters raised concerns about limitations: the conceptual leap of treating all time‑series as a single bucket, the lack of transparency or observability into the underlying dynamical system (i.e., it being a black‑box API), dependence on a remote service that could be a single point of failure, and the restrictive licensing that prevents open‑weight usage. Overall, the discussion suggests that the community sees promise in Timestral’s approach but believes important challenges—interpretability, reliability, licensing, and clear evaluation methodology—still need to be addressed.

stories.author: zoozla
stories.title: Show HN: WhatsApp MCP running free on Cloudflare
stories.groq_label: WhatsApp messages are scraped via the Web protocol into a Cloudflare Durable Object, enabling AI agents to query personal chat history without sending.
stories.groq_discussion: This Show HN: WhatsApp MCP running free on Cloudflare aims to solve the problem of giving users a personal AI assistant that can read and send WhatsApp messages through a free Cloudflare‑hosted service. The Hacker News discussion was mixed, with many commenters appreciating the novelty and low‑effort setup, highlighting strengths such as easy deployment, integration with local AI models, and the potential to build context‑aware bots. At the same time, several commenters raised concerns about privacy (messages being exposed to third‑party AI training data), violation of WhatsApp’s terms of service and the risk of account bans, and the broader issue of further centralising personal communications. Overall, the community sees the project as an interesting proof‑of‑concept with useful capabilities, but stresses that privacy, compliance, and reliability challenges must be addressed for wider adoption.
stories.groq_explain: A small server you host on Cloudflare lets an AI assistant read and search your personal WhatsApp chats. You link your phone once like WhatsApp Web; the server pulls new messages once a day, stores them in a private SQLite DB, and lets any MCP‑compatible client (Claude, etc.) query your history—e.g., “what did Dana say about the flights?” or “summarize the family group this week.” It never sends messages, only reads. It matters because it gives you AI‑driven insight into your own messaging data without relying on third‑party services, while keeping the data confined to your Cloudflare account. However, it uses unofficial WhatsApp Web protocols, so it technically violates WhatsApp’s terms.

stories.author: amrrs
stories.title: If you don't run your own LLM proxy, how do you know whats going on?
stories.groq_label: Debate centers on self‑hosted LLM proxies for transparent metrics versus opaque, costly API‑key subscriptions.
stories.groq_discussion:
This discussion aims to solve the problem of monitoring what LLM agents are doing when you don’t run your own proxy. The Hacker News discussion was generally mixed, with many commenters appreciating the added observability, security, and cost‑tracking that self‑hosted proxies (e.g., LiteLLM, agentsview, Aperture) provide. They highlighted strengths such as full API metrics in a GUI, the ability to issue virtual keys so real provider keys never touch sandboxes, and fine‑grained guardrails that make orchestration safer.

At the same time, several commenters raised concerns about the complexity and maintenance overhead of running a proxy, the brittleness of existing proxy implementations, and the question of whether the effort is worth it for typical home‑use subscriptions that feel “effectively infinite.” A few pointed out the high cost of using API keys versus flat‑rate subscriptions, while others noted that commercial services like OpenRouter already bundle the needed monitoring features.

Overall, the discussion suggests that the community sees value in running a personal LLM proxy for better insight and control, but it also recognizes that the added operational burden and potential instability may make it unnecessary for many users, especially those on modest personal workloads.

stories.author: allinonai
stories.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: LLM agents that think in latent space, act through text
stories.groq_label: Hybrid agents loop latent representations from the final transformer layer to perform internal reasoning before emitting text, boosting performance beyond pure token‑based generation.
stories.groq_discussion:
This research paper introduces hybrid reasoning agents that combine latent‑space reasoning with traditional text‑based interaction, aiming to overcome the limitations of pure‑language reasoning in large language models. The Hacker News discussion was generally mixed‑positive. Many commenters praised the innovative approach, highlighting strengths such as the potential for faster and higher‑quality reasoning, the ability to keep intermediate thoughts in latent space (reducing verbose restatements), and the promise of applying the technique to upcoming models like Qwen 3.8 27B. Several participants noted that the concept aligns with intuitive ideas about how future frontier models might operate and could enable richer tool use beyond plain text.

At the same time, commenters raised several concerns. Some questioned the practical implementation, pointing out that the current system only loops over the final layer and wondering whether earlier layers might yield better transformations. Others reported performance problems when running the 14 B model in llama.cpp, suggesting that the integration may need refinement. Comparisons to similar architectures such as Astra’s looped transformer were requested, and there were calls for clearer explanations of how latent reasoning is converted back into human‑readable text. A few users also cautioned that the evaluation section was limited and that more extensive benchmarks would be needed to confirm the claimed benefits.

Overall, the community sees the hybrid reasoning idea as promising and potentially impactful, but consensus is that further engineering work, broader evaluation, and clearer documentation are required before the approach can be widely adopted.

stories.groq_explain: Free Pascal’s compiler and Lazarus IDE now fully support dynamic packages, letting developers create and install components, controls, and extensions as shared libraries without recompiling the whole IDE. This enables fast plugin development, easier distribution of code as separate modules, and the ability to replace parts of an application at runtime, making development and deployment more flexible and efficient.

stories.author: fagnerbrack
stories.title: DeepSeek search and fetch – $0.75 per 1000 successful requests
stories.groq_label: DeepSeek's $0.75 per 1 000 query price undercuts rivals, sparking debate over anti‑bot effectiveness and completeness of fetched content.
stories.groq_discussion:
This service aims to provide an inexpensive web‑search‑and‑fetch API for language‑model agents, pricing the search at $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests. The Hacker News discussion was generally mixed, with many commenters appreciating the very low cost, the competitive pricing compared with Brave, Kagi and other providers, and the fact that the offering appears to work well enough to replace older LLM‑search routines in daily use. Participants also highlighted the usefulness of a cheap search endpoint for agent‑driven applications and noted that DeepSeek’s “Flash” model makes the search component stand out among current offerings.

At the same time, several commenters raised concerns about reliability and coverage. Questions were raised about how the service handles anti‑bot protections such as Cloudflare challenges, with some wondering whether it returns errors, empty results, or the desired content. Users reported that politically sensitive queries often return zero results, that the fetch endpoint sometimes returns only plain text without hyperlinks, and that the underlying infrastructure (apparently Huawei Cloud in Hong Kong) may impose regional restrictions or censorship. There was also confusion about exactly what the product is and how it differs from self‑hosted alternatives like searxng‑ai‑kit, leading some to view it as a re‑branding of older Google Search API concepts.

Overall, the community sees promise in the ultra‑low‑price model and its potential for agent‑centric workflows, but many feel that the service needs better handling of anti‑bot barriers, clearer documentation, and more robust result quality before it can be widely adopted.
